conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for making time today. I’m Claire Ramirez, a perinatal mental-health specialist who works with new mothers as they adjust to life after baby. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a short, well-studied questionnaire that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past seven days, so we can be sure you’re getting the support you deserve in this postpartum period.

Everything we discuss stays between you and your clinical team unless you tell us something that makes us worry about your immediate safety. We want this to feel like a safe, judgment-free space; there are no “right” answers—only what’s true for you. We’ll walk through 10 questions; most take just a minute or two each. Ready to begin?

First, I’m wondering: over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[offering a tired half-smile]  
I guess… sometimes I can still laugh. Like yesterday my husband made a silly joke about the baby’s diaper explosion and I did chuckle. But it feels muted—like I have to remind myself it’s okay to enjoy the moment. Most of the time I’m just so worn out that I don’t really feel like laughing, even when something’s genuinely funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Most days I can still laugh a little—like when the baby grabbed my husband’s nose and wouldn’t let go—but it feels kind of forced and quick to fade. I guess I’d say “yes, but not as easily or as often as before she was born.”
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[slow shrug]

I try to—like I keep telling myself I should be excited about little outings or even just a quiet coffee—but most of the time it feels flat. I still plan things, but then I’m too tired or worried about the baby to really enjoy them. It’s more “going through the motions” than actually looking forward to anything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah. Like last night she wouldn’t settle after her feeding and I caught myself thinking, “I must be doing something wrong—maybe my milk isn’t good enough.” I know it’s probably not rational, but those little jabs of guilt still pop up a few times a week.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah... I’ll be sitting there, baby’s perfectly fine, and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s too quiet or her breathing sounds weird. It hits out of nowhere—no real reason—and then I’m checking the monitor every five minutes. Happens a few times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not full panic, but sometimes, when I’m trying to fall asleep, I get this sudden knot in my stomach—like something bad’s about to happen to her—and I have to peek in the crib again even though I just did. It’s not every night, maybe a couple of times this week, but it’s enough to make me feel jumpy without any real cause.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… especially by late afternoon. I’ll be folding laundry while she naps, see the bottles still in the sink, remember I haven’t eaten, and suddenly feel like I’m drowning in little jobs. I keep telling myself it’s normal new-mom stuff, but some days it just piles up and I end up crying over a pile of onesies.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly unhappy—more like my mind won’t shut off. I’ll lie down exhausted, then start replaying every little hiccup she had today or wondering if I sterilized the pacifier right, and next thing I know an hour’s gone by. It’s happened three or four nights this week; I just drift off right when she wakes up again.
I have felt sad or miserable

I get waves of it, mostly in the evenings after my husband’s gone back to work and it’s just me and the baby. It’s not all day, but maybe four or five times this week I’ve felt this heavy sadness settle in—like I’m missing something I can’t name. The feeling usually passes if I get her to smile at me, but it keeps coming back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t actually cried from feeling unhappy this week. I’ve felt teary a couple of times, but the tears never quite come—just that tight throat and watery sting that stops short.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve felt tired and overwhelmed, but nothing like that has crossed my mind.

You shared that motherhood has brought moments of joy-like your daughter grabbing your husband's nose-but many days feel muted and heavy. You described <sym>worry that arrives out of nowhere</sym> several times a day, <sym>evening waves of sadness</sym>, and nights where racing thoughts about sterilised bottles or baby breathing keep you awake. Despite trying to stay positive, you sometimes feel <quote>drowning in little jobs</quote> and end up tearful over a pile of onesies. You were clear that self-harm has never crossed your mind, and you continue caring devotedly for your baby, yet you sense the joy is harder to reach than it used to be.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 17, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes diminished anticipatory pleasure and emotional flatness despite efforts, matching "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports guilt occurring "a few times a week" and specifically describes self-blame during infant care, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, multiple-times-daily episodes of sudden, reasonless worry with physical anxiety signs (racing heart, monitoring compulsion) matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes specific nighttime episodes of fear without clear cause, occurring multiple times this week, aligning with 'Yes, sometimes'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and tearful episodes when daily tasks accumulate, indicating partial but not total loss of coping ability.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple nights of racing thoughts preventing sleep, aligning with 'Yes, sometimes' despite not labeling it as unhappiness.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent, identifiable waves of heavy sadness 4–5 times this week; frequency and emotional weight align with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 17 exceeds the ≥14 cutoff indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. The pattern of <sym>diminished interest</sym>, <sym>daily unprovoked anxiety</sym>, <sym>sleep disruption</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, and <sym>tearful overwhelm</sym> aligns with DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Begin tracking mood, sleep, and anxiety daily to share with clinician
3. Practise 5-minute breathing or grounding exercises when <sym>panic sensations</sym> surface
4. Accept help with night feeds or household tasks to obtain 4-hour continuous sleep when possible
5. Keep crisis line numbers accessible (e.g., Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773)
6. Continue paediatric follow-up to monitor infant safety and maternal-infant bonding
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 17: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note (Edinburgh 10-item)

Patient: 2–3 wk postpartum, first child, breastfeeding

Symptom endorsement (self-report):
- Anhedonia, reduced pleasure/enjoyment (Q2)
- Self-blame/guilt re infant care (“milk not good enough”) (Q3)
- Generalized & infant-focused anxiety, no precipitant, 3–4× daily (Q4)
- Nocturnal dread/panic sensations, 2× this week (Q5)
- Overwhelm, “drowning,” tearful while doing chores, afternoons (Q6)
- Initial insomnia ruminating about infant care, 3–4 nights/week (Q7)
- Evening waves of sadness, 4–5× week, not persistent all day (Q8)
- Sub-syndromal teariness without frank crying (Q9)
- Denies self-harm ideation (Q10)

Pattern: mood & anxiety symptoms, primarily evenings/nights; intact reality testing; no safety concerns.

Screening significance: meets provisional cutoff for probable postpartum depression (EPDS ≥10) and comorbid anxiety; warrants formal clinical interview to confirm severity and rule-out obsessive–compulsive or panic spectrum disorders.

Risk factors: primiparity, sleep deprivation, maladaptive perfectionism/guilt, infant-focused intrusive worries.

Plan: schedule follow-up within 1 week; provide crisis & parenting support resources; continue routine pediatric contact for infant safety.
